title: Why Is the Turkey Bird Named After a Country?
hook: The turkey was named after a country it never came from. Worse, it wasn't even the first bird to get that name.
thumbnail_picture: Big and close on the right: a giant bronze turkey with its tail fanned wide, standing beside a tiny speckled guinea fowl. A 1500s European farmer in a wide-brimmed hat stares at the two birds with his mouth open in shock. Warm golden sunset light in a farmyard. The left third of the frame stays empty.
description:
Why is the turkey bird named after a country? It's a 500-year-old mix-up that crossed the Mediterranean and the Atlantic: an African bird, Turkish-linked trade, a Mexican bird, and a country that finally changed its name to Türkiye.

Follow the name from African grassland to an imagined Istanbul bazaar, a Spanish dock, an English farmyard and back across the Atlantic, and see how the country's own name changed in 2022.

Sources worth checking: the Oxford English Dictionary entry for "turkey"; Carl Linnaeus, Systema Naturae, 10th edition (1758); the United Nations' June 2022 recognition of "Türkiye"; the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History on the domestication of the turkey.
tags: why is the turkey bird named turkey
why did turkey change its name to turkiye

scenes.narration: The turkey on your dinner table is named after a country it never came from. Worse, it wasn't even the first bird to get that name.
scenes.delivery: intriguing, plain and punchy, a half-smile
scenes.caption: THE WRONG NAME
scenes.picture: Close-up of a golden roasted turkey on a wooden dinner table, steam rising, candlelit warm light, with blurry hands of a family reaching in from the soft background.

scenes.narration: So which bird had the name first? And how did a whole country end up sharing its name with dinner?
scenes.caption: TWO BIRDS
scenes.picture: A roast turkey and a much smaller speckled roast guinea fowl side by side on a wooden table, soft window light, one curious hand hovering above them.

scenes.narration: To find out, we have to chase one name across the Mediterranean, and twice across the Atlantic. It changes hands at every stop.
scenes.caption: THE JOURNEY
scenes.picture: Wide sunrise view of a wooden trading ship with billowing sails leaving a Mediterranean harbour with stone quays, gulls overhead, golden water, 1500s.

scenes.narration: Our trail starts in Africa, on dry grassland at sunrise, where a flock of loud, spotty birds scratches the dust.
scenes.caption: AFRICA
scenes.picture: A flock of grey spotted guinea fowl scratching in the dust of a dry African grassland at sunrise, acacia trees on the horizon, golden low light.

scenes.narration: These are guinea fowl: grey feathers freckled with white, a bony blue head, and a shriek that carries far.
scenes.caption: GUINEA FOWL
scenes.picture: Close-up of one guinea fowl with grey feathers dotted white, a bare blue head and a bony crest, beak wide open mid-shriek, blurred grass behind.

scenes.narration: The Romans loved them. Wealthy families kept guinea fowl in their courtyards and served them at feasts.
scenes.caption: ROME, 100 AD
scenes.picture: A Roman villa courtyard with stone columns, a woman with pinned-up brown hair in a cream tunic scattering grain for guinea fowl pecking at her feet, sunny afternoon, 100 AD.

scenes.narration: But when Rome fell, the courtyards emptied, and the bird largely disappeared from European farms.
scenes.caption: FORGOTTEN
scenes.picture: An overgrown, crumbling Roman villa courtyard with broken columns, an empty wooden bird pen, weeds and drifting mist, grey morning light, about 600 AD.

scenes.narration: Then, in the 1400s, it came back. Packed in crates, squawking all the way, it arrived by sea.
scenes.caption: THE COMEBACK
scenes.picture: Wooden crates full of speckled birds stacked on the deck of a Mediterranean trading galley, two sailors in simple 1400s tunics hauling ropes, bright blue sea.

scenes.narration: The likeliest story is that the birds came through Mediterranean trade that Turkish merchants were part of. Portuguese ships also brought them straight from West Africa.
scenes.caption: TURKISH TRADE
scenes.picture: A busy eastern Mediterranean harbour at dawn, domed mosques and slim minarets on the hills, wooden ships at a stone quay, porters carrying crates of birds, 1400s.

scenes.narration: Some may have gone overland instead, by camel caravan up through Egypt and Syria, toward the busy ports of the coast.
scenes.caption: BY CAMEL
scenes.picture: A camel caravan crossing golden desert dunes, wicker cages of speckled guinea fowl strapped to the camels, a robed driver with a headcloth walking alongside, hazy sun, 1400s.

scenes.narration: Picture a bazaar like Istanbul's, where a merchant haggles over a crate of spotted birds, between sacks of spice and copper pots.
scenes.caption: IMAGINED BAZAAR
scenes.picture: An Ottoman merchant with a white turban, grey beard and long striped robe haggling with a European buyer in a dark cap over a wooden crate of guinea fowl, sacks of spice and copper pots, bazaar arches behind.

scenes.narration: Buyers in Europe never saw where the birds were born. All they saw was a trade that ran through Turkish hands.
scenes.caption: WHO SOLD THEM
scenes.picture: Close-up of two hands passing silver coins over a crate of speckled birds in a market, one hand in a rich embroidered robe sleeve, the other in a plain wool sleeve.

scenes.narration: So Europeans likely called them turkey hens, either because of Turkish-controlled trade, or because 'Turkey' simply meant 'exotic'. Either way, the name rode the crates all the way to England.
scenes.caption: TURKEY HENS
scenes.picture: A merchant ship laden with wooden crates sailing toward a grey English coast with white cliffs at sunset, long orange light on the sails, 1500s.

scenes.narration: The birds were a pricey, exotic dish for the wealthy, so a bird from far away fit perfectly.
scenes.caption: ENGLAND, 1540
scenes.picture: A Tudor market stall where a seller in a wool cap holds up a speckled guinea fowl, a wealthy woman in a fine green gown inspecting it, wooden stalls and cobbles, about 1540.

scenes.narration: That should have settled it. One bird, one name, a happy ending. <short pause> But then the Atlantic got involved.
scenes.caption: A SECOND BIRD
scenes.picture: A Spanish caravel riding a big swell on the open Atlantic under dark, dramatic storm clouds, a single shaft of light falling on its sails, about 1520.

scenes.narration: On the far side of that ocean, in Mexico, people had raised a giant, bronze-feathered bird long before any European showed up.
scenes.caption: MEXICO
scenes.picture: An Aztec woman with long black braided hair and a plain white cotton dress feeding large bronze-feathered turkeys in a village yard, adobe houses and maize fields behind, warm morning, about 1500.

scenes.narration: It had a red, wrinkled neck, a huge fan of tail feathers, and enough meat to feed a whole family.
scenes.caption: THE BIG BIRD
scenes.picture: Close-up of a male turkey with a red wrinkled neck and a huge fanned tail of bronze feathers, strutting in a dusty Mexican village yard, adobe wall blurred behind.

scenes.narration: The Aztecs called the bird totolin, and the male huexolotl. No India, no Turkey, no Africa. Just a bird.
scenes.caption: HUEXOLOTL
scenes.picture: An Aztec woman with long black braided hair and a plain white cotton dress gently holding a large bronze turkey in her arms, smiling, stone steps and maize stalks behind her.

scenes.narration: In the early 1500s, Spanish sailors saw how much meat those birds carried, so they loaded cages of them onto their ships.
scenes.caption: SPANISH SHIPS
scenes.picture: Spanish sailors in 1500s shirts and caps carrying wooden cages of large bronze turkeys up a gangplank onto a caravel on a sandy tropical shore, palm trees, morning haze.

scenes.narration: Weeks in a rolling, stuffy hold. But the birds that survived would change European menus forever.
scenes.caption: THE CROSSING
scenes.picture: Inside a dim wooden ship's hold lit by one swinging lantern, cages of bronze turkeys stacked among barrels, feathers drifting through the air, about 1520.

scenes.narration: Finally, the cages thumped onto a dock in Spain, and the birds blinked into the sunlight.
scenes.caption: SPAIN
scenes.picture: Wooden cages of big bronze turkeys being set down on a sunny stone dock in Seville by two dockworkers in wide hats, tall ship masts behind, about 1520.

scenes.narration: From there the birds spread north. In England, people who knew guinea fowl saw the new bird, decided it was the same sort of thing, and called it 'turkey' too.
scenes.caption: A FAMILIAR FACE?
scenes.picture: A middle-aged English farmer with a ruddy face, brown wool cap and mud-brown tunic frowning with his hand on his chin, looking over a wooden pen holding a big bronze turkey and a small speckled guinea fowl, thatched barn behind.

scenes.narration: Sure, this one was far bigger. Sure, it came from the west, not the east. But close enough.
scenes.caption: CLOSE ENOUGH
scenes.picture: Side-by-side close-up of a huge bronze turkey head and a small spotted guinea fowl head, both bare-necked, facing each other in a farmyard, soft light.

scenes.narration: So the name jumped. The giant bird from Mexico became a 'turkey' too, and nobody stopped to check.
scenes.caption: THE NAME JUMPS
scenes.picture: A middle-aged English farmer with a ruddy face, brown wool cap and mud-brown tunic proudly holding up a big bronze turkey in a muddy farmyard, chickens scattering, thatched cottage behind.

scenes.narration: Soon the new birds were spreading through Spain, France, and England, carried on carts down muddy country roads.
scenes.caption: SPREADING
scenes.picture: A horse-drawn wooden cart loaded with cages of turkeys rolling down a muddy country road past green fields, a driver in a straw hat, cloudy sky, 1530s.

scenes.narration: Meanwhile, the speckled African bird got a consolation prize: 'guinea fowl', after the West African coast Portuguese ships brought it from.
scenes.caption: GUINEA FOWL
scenes.picture: A Portuguese caravel anchored off a palm-lined West African beach, small rowing boats carrying cages of speckled guinea fowl toward the ship, hot bright sky, about 1500.

scenes.narration: By the 1540s, roasted turkeys were turning up at rich people's feasts, steaming on platters under candlelight.
scenes.caption: THE FEAST
scenes.picture: A candlelit Tudor great hall where two noblemen in feathered hats sit at a long wooden table, a roasted turkey steaming on a silver platter in the centre, about 1540.

scenes.narration: By the 1600s, the bird was showing up at wealthy English Christmas tables.
scenes.caption: CHRISTMAS
scenes.picture: A snowy English village street at dusk, a woman in a grey wool cloak carrying a plucked turkey home past glowing windows of timbered houses, about 1600.

scenes.narration: One name was now stuck on two completely different birds, from two completely different continents.
scenes.caption: ONE NAME, TWO BIRDS
scenes.picture: A speckled guinea fowl and a big bronze turkey standing side by side on a wooden farm fence at dawn, mist drifting over the fields behind.

scenes.narration: Even clever people couldn't keep them straight. Old books use 'turkey' for both, and historians still argue over which bird they mean.
scenes.caption: STILL ARGUING
scenes.picture: A scholar in a dark Tudor gown and flat cap in a candlelit study, leaning over a table where a live guinea fowl and a live turkey stand together, his eyebrows raised in confusion.

scenes.narration: And as the bird spread, everyone who met it blamed somewhere else for it.
scenes.caption: BLAME GAME
scenes.picture: A European market square, 1550s, where two traders in hats point in opposite directions while a customer in the middle holds up a big turkey with a baffled look.

scenes.narration: The French called it the 'chicken of India', because early explorers thought the New World was part of India.
scenes.caption: FRANCE
scenes.picture: A French kitchen with copper pans hanging on the wall, a cook in a white apron plucking a turkey over a wooden table, glowing fireplace behind, about 1550.

scenes.narration: The Portuguese said 'Peru'. The Dutch named it after Calicut, a port city in India.
scenes.caption: PERU? CALICUT?
scenes.picture: A Dutch merchant in a black hat and white collar standing at a wooden table with a roasted bird on a plate, canal houses and boats visible through the window, about 1600.

scenes.narration: And in Turkey itself? Turkish cooks called the bird 'hindi', which means Indian. Even the supposed home blamed India.
scenes.caption: HINDI
scenes.picture: An Ottoman cook in a tall white hat in a steamy palace kitchen, lifting a large roasted bird from a copper pot, copper pans and arched windows around him, about 1550.

scenes.narration: Nobody was lying. They were all guessing, and a bird that crosses oceans leaves a very messy trail.
scenes.caption: A MESSY TRAIL
scenes.picture: A foggy harbour at dawn crowded with many wooden ships of different sizes, lanterns glowing through the mist, gulls circling, 1500s.

scenes.narration: Then the name made one last trip, back across the Atlantic, on small English ships crowded with colonists: first to Virginia in 1607, then to Plymouth in 1620.
scenes.caption: BACK ACROSS
scenes.picture: A small English sailing ship crowded with colonists in plain wool clothes, riding grey Atlantic waves under a wide pale sky, 1620.

scenes.narration: Hungry, seasick, and an ocean from home, they stepped ashore into a forest none of them knew.
scenes.caption: NEW SHORE
scenes.picture: Three tired English colonists in plain 1600s wool coats wading through shallow water to a forested shore, tall dark trees ahead, misty late-autumn morning, 1620.

scenes.narration: Picture it: something moves in the trees, and they freeze. A huge bronze bird is strutting like it owns the place.
scenes.caption: SOMETHING MOVES
scenes.picture: A wild turkey with bronze feathers strutting at the edge of an autumn forest, while a bearded English colonist in a grey wool cap and plain brown wool coat stands frozen mid-step with wide shocked eyes.

scenes.narration: They knew exactly what to call it. Back home, people had been saying 'turkey' for decades, and the colonists' own writings call these wild birds turkeys.
scenes.caption: THEY KNEW IT
scenes.picture: Close-up of a bearded English colonist in a grey wool cap and plain brown wool coat, pointing off to the side with a delighted, amazed face, autumn trees behind, 1620.

scenes.narration: For people just off a long voyage, that bird wasn't a curiosity. It was dinner.
scenes.caption: DINNER
scenes.picture: A bearded English colonist in a grey wool cap and plain brown wool coat crouched beside a campfire turning a wooden spit with a large roasting bird, dusk light, smoke curling into the trees.

scenes.narration: Native peoples across much of the continent had hunted that bird for thousands of years, with names of their own.
scenes.caption: OLDER NAMES
scenes.picture: A Native American hunter in deerskin clothing quietly crouching with a bow in an autumn forest, watching a wild turkey in the fallen leaves ahead, before 1500.

scenes.narration: So the name had come full circle, landing back on the very continent the bird came from. Wrong name, right bird.
scenes.caption: FULL CIRCLE
scenes.picture: A flock of wild turkeys walking through golden autumn forest light, wide shot, leaves falling, North America.

scenes.narration: But science only made it messier. In 1758, the Swedish naturalist Linnaeus gave the turkey the genus name Meleagris.
scenes.caption: LINNAEUS, 1758
scenes.picture: A Swedish naturalist with a white powdered wig and a dark 1700s coat sitting at a candlelit desk, studying a stuffed bronze turkey with a magnifying glass, shelves of specimens behind him.

scenes.narration: Meleagris is the old Greek word for guinea fowl, and the species name of the helmeted guinea fowl. So even in science, the two birds share a word.
scenes.caption: MELEAGRIS
scenes.picture: Close-up of a hand holding a quill pen resting on a desk beside a spotted guinea fowl feather and a bronze turkey feather, candlelight, 1758.

scenes.narration: But the puzzle has a second half. What happened to the country that got dragged into all this?
scenes.caption: THE COUNTRY
scenes.picture: Istanbul skyline at dawn with domes and minarets above the Bosphorus, ferries crossing the pink water, soft morning haze.

scenes.narration: To medieval Europeans, the lands ruled by Turkish dynasties were 'Turchia', the land of the Turks.
scenes.caption: TURCHIA
scenes.picture: A medieval European traveller in a hooded brown cloak riding a mule along a dusty road through Anatolian hills, a stone caravanserai in the distance, about 1300.

scenes.narration: That's where the English word Turkey comes from. It's centuries older than any bird dinner.
scenes.caption: OLDER THAN THE BIRD
scenes.picture: A camel caravan crossing a high Anatolian mountain pass at sunset, long shadows on the road, snow on the peaks, about 1300.

scenes.narration: In 1923, after the sultanate had been abolished, a republic was proclaimed. In Turkish its name was Türkiye.
scenes.picture: A group of men in fezzes, sheepskin caps and army uniforms cheering and tossing their caps in the air in a dusty Ankara street, early morning sun, 1923.

scenes.narration: But English speakers kept the old name. So for about a hundred years, a nation and a roast dinner shared one word.
scenes.caption: ONE WORD, TWO THINGS
scenes.picture: An English butcher's shop in the 1930s with plucked turkeys hanging in a row from hooks, a butcher in a striped apron smiling in the doorway.

scenes.narration: Turkish officials argued the English word had picked up silly meanings, from the bird to a slang word for a flop.
scenes.caption: A BAD LOOK
scenes.picture: A Turkish official in a dark suit at a tidy desk, staring unimpressed at a plate holding a roast turkey drumstick, a modern office window behind him.

scenes.narration: Imagine telling people where you're from, and hearing nothing back but 'gobble, gobble'.
scenes.caption: GOBBLE GOBBLE
scenes.picture: A young Turkish man at a café table looking exasperated while a tourist across from him flaps his arms like wings and laughs, tea glasses on the table.

scenes.narration: So in December 2021, a presidential circular told exporters and officials to use 'Türkiye', and Turkey asked the world to follow.
scenes.caption: A NEW REQUEST
scenes.picture: A man in a dark suit speaking at a wooden podium in a grand government hall, microphones in front of him, rows of listeners seated blurred behind.

scenes.narration: From then on, 'Made in Türkiye' was the label meant for goods, from carpets to washing machines.
scenes.caption: MADE IN TÜRKİYE
scenes.picture: A factory worker in a safety vest lifting a rolled carpet onto a pallet beside a stack of washing machines in a bright modern warehouse.

scenes.narration: In June 2022, the United Nations agreed to the change. Officially, the country had stepped out from the bird's shadow.
scenes.caption: JUNE 2022
scenes.picture: A wide hall of delegates in suits applauding in a modern assembly chamber, soft golden light from tall windows, flags softly blurred.

scenes.narration: It's pronounced roughly 'TEWR-kee-yeh', with a rounded 'ew' sound. Say it out loud. It sounds nothing like a bird.
scenes.caption: SAY IT
scenes.picture: A friendly teacher speaking to a few smiling students in a bright modern classroom, one student repeating a word with a grin, mouth rounded.

scenes.narration: Did the whole world switch? Not quite. Many English speakers, dictionaries, and holiday menus still say turkey.
scenes.caption: STILL TURKEY
scenes.picture: A family laughing around a holiday dinner table with a big roast turkey in the centre, warm lamplight, a window showing dusk.

scenes.narration: In short: Europeans likely named an African bird after the Turkish trade that brought it, then gave that name to a Mexican one.
scenes.caption: THE MIX-UP
scenes.picture: A wooden merchant ship loaded with crates of speckled birds sailing across a bright blue sea toward a distant coast, wide calm sky, 1500s.

scenes.narration: The country never chose the name, never claimed either bird, and in its own language, called the big one Indian.
scenes.caption: NOT ITS FAULT
scenes.picture: A relaxed man in modern clothes sipping tea from a small glass on an Istanbul rooftop terrace at dusk, domes and the glittering Bosphorus behind him.

scenes.narration: And the bird that started it all? Guinea fowl still patrol farmyards today, shrieking at every stranger who walks past.
scenes.caption: STILL SCREAMING
scenes.picture: A flock of guinea fowl in a farmyard at dusk, one with its neck stretched high and beak open mid-shriek, a farm gate and barn behind.

scenes.narration: So when a turkey lands on your table, remember: that name crossed continents and the Atlantic, and was a mistake along most of the way.
scenes.caption: MOSTLY WRONG
scenes.picture: A wild turkey standing on a grassy ridge at sunset, wide shot, its tail fanned in golden light, hills stretching to the horizon.

narrator: Adventurous travel-documentary narrator, energetic and warm, a sense of motion and discovery.

short.title: Why Is the Turkey Bird Named After a Country?
short.description:
Your dinner turkey is named after the country Turkey, but it came from Mexico. Here's the mix-up that put one name on two birds.
Turkey bird name origin, guinea fowl, Türkiye and a very old mistake.

scenes.narration: The turkey bird is named after Turkey, but it comes from Mexico. So why?
scenes.caption: WRONG NAME
scenes.picture: A golden roasted turkey large and central on a wooden dinner table, steam rising, warm candlelight, two family hands reaching in from a blurry background, simple cozy dining room, tall portrait framing

scenes.narration: In the 1400s, Europeans bought African guinea fowl through Turkish trade routes.
scenes.caption: 1400S TRADE
scenes.picture: A speckled grey guinea fowl crate stack large in the frame on a stone quay of an Ottoman Mediterranean harbour at dawn, a porter in a white turban and plain tunic lifting one crate, domes and masts behind, 1400s

scenes.narration: Buyers never saw where the birds began, so they called them turkey hens.
scenes.caption: TURKEY HENS
scenes.picture: Close-up of a puzzled European buyer, middle-aged man with a brown wool cap and brown tunic, holding a speckled guinea fowl above a crate, beside a smiling Turkish merchant with a turban and long robe, busy 1400s market, simple background

scenes.narration: In England, those birds were pricey food for the rich.
scenes.caption: ENGLAND, 1540
scenes.picture: A wealthy Tudor woman in a rich red gown and white headdress leaning in to inspect a speckled guinea fowl held up by a market seller in a wool cap, wooden stall, cobbled street, England 1540

scenes.narration: But in the early 1500s, Spanish sailors brought a giant Mexican bird to Spain.
scenes.caption: A 2ND BIRD
scenes.picture: A big wooden cage holding huge bronze-feathered turkeys, central on a sunny stone dock in Seville, two Spanish sailors in 1500s caps and loose shirts lifting it, ship masts and blue sky behind, about 1520

scenes.narration: English farmers thought the Mexican bird looked like guinea fowl.
scenes.caption: CLOSE ENOUGH?
scenes.picture: Close-up of a frowning Tudor farmer, stocky middle-aged man with a brown wool cap and rough brown tunic, hand on chin, staring at a pen holding a big bronze turkey beside a small speckled guinea fowl, thatched barn behind

scenes.narration: So they called it turkey too, and nobody checked.
scenes.caption: NAME JUMPS
scenes.picture: A proud Tudor farmer, stocky middle-aged man with a brown wool cap and rough brown tunic, holding up a huge bronze turkey with both arms in a muddy farmyard, chickens scattering, filling the tall frame

scenes.narration: Now one name sat on two birds, one African, one Mexican.
scenes.caption: ONE NAME
scenes.picture: A speckled grey guinea fowl and a big bronze turkey standing side by side on a wooden farm fence at dawn, both large and central in the frame, soft mist and green fields behind, England

scenes.narration: Colonists carried that name across the Atlantic to Plymouth in 1620.
scenes.caption: PLYMOUTH, 1620
scenes.picture: A small English wooden sailing ship with square sails, central and large, riding rough grey Atlantic waves under a pale cloudy sky, tired colonists in plain dark wool clothes huddled on deck, 1620

scenes.narration: But wild turkeys already lived there.
scenes.caption: FULL CIRCLE
scenes.picture: A wild turkey with bronze feathers strutting large in the foreground at the edge of an autumn forest, an English colonist in a plain wool cap and dark coat standing frozen with wide shocked eyes behind it, Plymouth 1620

scenes.narration: So Europeans likely named an African bird after Turkish trade, then gave that name to Mexico's bird.
scenes.caption: THE MIX-UP
scenes.picture: A wild turkey standing large and close on a grassy ridge at sunset, its tail fanned wide in golden light, rolling hills stretching softly behind, calm peaceful mood
